preamble: Depalatalization (hardening) of the palatalized alveolar fricative [sʲ] to plain [s] removes the palatal secondary articulation. In East Slavic, consonants were positionally palatalized before front vowels in Old East Slavic; Ukrainian later hardened them before /e/ (село [seˈɫɔ] against Russian [sʲɪˈɫo]). In Russian itself, the reflexive postfix -ся/-сь has a hard [s] variant that formed part of the Old Moscow orthoepic norm and survives variably in the speech of many speakers.

examples.note: Old East Slavic softened /s/ before /e/ (9th c. /sɛˈloː/ > 11th c. /sʲɛˈloː/); Ukrainian hardened it again, whereas Russian keeps [sʲɪˈɫo].
In older and dialectal pronunciation the reflexive postfix is hard; the hard [s] is commonest after velarized [ɫ] in masculine past-tense forms such as боя́лся 'he was afraid'.

sources: Belyaev, D. D. (2023). Reflexive Postfix: Between Softness and Hardness. Trudy Instituta russkogo jazyka im. V. V. Vinogradova 4(38), 11–24. https://doi.org/10.31912/pvrli-2023.4.1
